title: Nvidia Shares Slide After Forecast Underwhelms Investors
content: Nvidia, the dominant maker of artificial intelligence chips, suffered its worst stock decline in 10 months after the company’s latest forecast failed to dispel fears of an AI bubble. The shares fell 5.5% to $184.89 in New York, marking the biggest one-day drop since April 16. The decline followed a first-quarter sales outlook that — on its face — looked impressive. Nvidia easily beat the average analyst estimate and delivered a 73% surge in fourth-quarter revenue. The reaction was a stark reminder of the skepticism now surrounding Nvidia. After explosive sales growth turned the chipmaker into the world’s most valuable company, investors are seeking stronger assurances that booming AI spending can be maintained. Bloomberg Intelligence Senior Semiconductor Analyst Kunjan Sobhani, and Senior Technology Credit Analyst Robert Schiffman both join Bloomberg Businessweek Daily to discuss. They speak with Carol Massar and Tim Stenovec. (Source: Bloomberg)

Bonnie Blue-Chip

An economically incoherent Substack post about AI went viral this week and we’re furious it wasn’t ours<https://substack.com/redirect/7ee24037-bf5c-4ec6-829e-ac5ac236e551?j=eyJ1IjoicDBzaDEifQ.aWeIhmNCVGNColYUmI1TE7JzeHpAMb4ONxSzBHYhJl4>.

For a catch-up on the Citrini Research story, go elsewhere<https://substack.com/redirect/e14ed215-42bc-46b5-9984-035a043debd2?j=eyJ1IjoicDBzaDEifQ.aWeIhmNCVGNColYUmI1TE7JzeHpAMb4ONxSzBHYhJl4>. No more needs to be said about its retelling of Busted’s “Year 3000” over multiple thousand portentous words. Arguably, a lot less could’ve been said. From The Economist<https://substack.com/redirect/f8dbf3c1-ad37-4db3-957e-ad688635dc70?j=eyJ1IjoicDBzaDEifQ.aWeIhmNCVGNColYUmI1TE7JzeHpAMb4ONxSzBHYhJl4> and Citadel Securities<https://substack.com/redirect/1c9ceda4-4208-4f5a-84a7-75310c4339cb?j=eyJ1IjoicDBzaDEifQ.aWeIhmNCVGNColYUmI1TE7JzeHpAMb4ONxSzBHYhJl4> to this guy<https://substack.com/redirect/9f6d1e68-2199-43d3-885c-edf59ae023d2?j=eyJ1IjoicDBzaDEifQ.aWeIhmNCVGNColYUmI1TE7JzeHpAMb4ONxSzBHYhJl4>, sensible voices have taken the bait and dunked on a central premise that can be summed up as: “What if lump-of-labour-fallacy but computers?”

Not that Citrini will care:

[https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!jg53!,w_1100,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fc24c0de8-9e2a-4345-98f6-03303404e1a7_957x684.png]<https://substack.com/redirect/730b81cb-c236-4b03-a053-c6a9c87f57bb?j=eyJ1IjoicDBzaDEifQ.aWeIhmNCVGNColYUmI1TE7JzeHpAMb4ONxSzBHYhJl4>

A related theme, particularly among investment bank analysts who went freelance, has been whether Citrini’s celebrity marks a tipping point for freelance analysis.

Rupak Ghose has a good post<https://substack.com/redirect/134f45bb-c55d-4760-95b8-e6817baef1d0?j=eyJ1IjoicDBzaDEifQ.aWeIhmNCVGNColYUmI1TE7JzeHpAMb4ONxSzBHYhJl4> about how independent authors are better placed than the sell-side because they bring personality and direct distribution to tell stories without being constrained by job title, word count, or institutional timidity. On our pixels, Marc Rubinstein complains about the petrifying effects of research unbundling and conflict disclosure rules<https://substack.com/redirect/d96c893f-ea12-4346-9158-ca8c56654601?j=eyJ1IjoicDBzaDEifQ.aWeIhmNCVGNColYUmI1TE7JzeHpAMb4ONxSzBHYhJl4>.

Add in the atrophy of long-only fund management and the emergence of pod shops, whose teams tend to prefer specifics to scenarios. Retail investors, an ever-growing segment of the market, have a revealed preference for stories. Opportunities have never been greater to take their money by auto-renewing monthly instalments.

But to present any of this as new would be a mistake. Proto-bloggers were talking their book on Usenet<https://substack.com/redirect/f2672724-93bd-4c56-9dae-a96cbb590ead?j=eyJ1IjoicDBzaDEifQ.aWeIhmNCVGNColYUmI1TE7JzeHpAMb4ONxSzBHYhJl4> more than 30 years ago, while the grubby business of investment newsletters is at least a century older. Underserved niches like short selling and forensic accounting are where independents thrive. Bonus season has always marked the start of an annual migration of analysts to freelance consultancy.

Sell-side research abides because its primary purpose is marketing. Some of the marketing is on behalf of other banking services, some is for clients who want a communications backchannel, and none of it makes sense without a cross-subsidy. Quality will continue to decline but it won’t fade away for the same reason that vibe-coders won’t displace Uber: the value isn’t in the product, it’s in the network of relationships and regulatory arbitrages formed by its creation.

That’s not to deny the room for improvement. Sell-side is a cludge of workarounds that, if it didn’t already exist, no sane person would think to invent. But windy postulating about industry trends never paid the bills. Banks give that stuff away while locking down what clients value: meeting invitations, forecast models, and specialist sales desk memos that say what the analyst can’t.

Meanwhile, here in the shallow end of the research pool, we’ll continue to live by the economics of OnlyFans, where 1 per cent of creators take 99 per cent of the money. A few accounts might eke out a living by appealing to some niche, while the unpopular majority tries to attract attention with increasingly extreme acts of shamelessness. The safest prediction is always that the future will be the same but worse; not much will change, but we’ll live underwater.
